findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The validator invokes BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs a DB read and a non-atomic read-modify-write save as a side effect of model validation. Every call to user.valid? (including multiple validations during one save attempt, and the failed save that follows) increments match_count and stamps last_match_at, skewing the statistics the model's own spec asserts; ops staff reading match_count get inflated numbers. The save also silently discards stats on a uniqueness race. Any operator relying on these counters for abuse analysis is bitten from the first deploy.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail has no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates the table. The entire feature ships inert: after deploying, blocked_emails is empty, should_block? always returns false, and no operator can add an entry without hand-crafted SQL, so the new migration, model, validator, and client-side rejectedEmails logic are dead code until a follow-up ships.

[ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails check reports the generic 'user.email.invalid' message for an email that was specifically blocked, and it never clears an entry once pushed. A user whose email was blocked (e.g., via a stale row or a do_nothing/whitelist misfire) is told their syntactically valid email is 'invalid' with no actionable reason, and because the entry persists for the controller's lifetime, correcting a transient server-side error still shows the email as invalid until the modal is recreated.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail table and model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path inserts rows, so the entire blocking feature is inert for operators. Site staff cannot add a blocked email without hand-writing SQL, so the new validation never blocks anything in practice; users get no protection until unrelated future code adds a writer.

[ADVISORY] The email validator (including the domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic moved out of user.rb) is gated on `if: :email_changed?`, so the whitelist/blacklist and BlockedEmail checks are silently skipped on any save where the email attribute is unchanged. Admins who blacklist a domain after users registered, or who add a BlockedEmail row, get no effect on existing accounts whose saves don't touch email — the old code had the same gate, but the PR's stated goal (blocking bad emails) is undermined because the blocked check inherits it.

[ADVISORY] The EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch with `should_block?` stubbed; the whitelist (`email_domains_whitelist`) and blacklist (`email_domains_blacklist`) branches — logic deleted from user.rb and re-implemented in this new class — have zero coverage, and no existing user spec is updated to prove the moved restriction logic still fires through `validates :email, email: true`. A regression in the migrated domain-restriction regex or the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` short-circuit (e.g. a syntax error or the SiteSetting branch inverting) ships undetected; sites relying on email_domains_blacklist silently stop filtering signups.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail lookup uses exact case-sensitive string match (`where(email: email)`) while user emails are commonly downcased before validation, so mixed-case input or differently-cased stored rows never match. A user typing Bad@Spammers.org bypasses a blocked_email row stored as bad@spammers.org and registers successfully; the spec suite never covers case variation.

[ADVISORY] The new `errors`/`values` payload in the failed-create response has no test, and the client-side consumer (`createAccountController` pushObject into rejectedEmails and the `rejectedEmails.@each` dependent-key revalidation) has no JS test, so the end-to-end blocked-email UX this PR exists to deliver is unverified. If `user.errors.to_hash` key shape (symbol vs string) or `result.values.email` presence drifts, the client silently never adds to rejectedEmails and the user sees only the generic failure flash — the feature's visible behavior regresses with no failing spec.

[ADVISORY] The rejected-email client check reports the generic 'user.email.invalid' reason instead of the new 'user.email.blocked' message the server defines, and no locale entry for a blocked-specific client message exists, so the user cannot distinguish a blocked address from a malformed one. A user whose email was blocked sees 'invalid' and keeps retrying variations that will also be blocked, with no indication the address is prohibited.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed populates it — so the feature ships inert. Site operators cannot actually block any email address; the entire validation path (BlockedEmail.should_block?) always returns false in production until unrelated future code is written, making the diff's core deliverable unusable as shipped.

[ADVISORY] The validator triggers a database write (match_count increment and last_match_at update via BlockedEmail.should_block?) as a side effect of model validation, which is validation logic performing statistics bookkeeping not requested by 'add comprehensive email validation'. Any code path that validates a User (including benign checks like form pre-validation or admin screens showing a user) increments match_count and issues writes; validation is no longer idempotent, and records validated on every save re-trigger save recursion risk on the BlockedEmail record within a User validation callback chain.

[ADVISORY] The failure response now exposes the raw errors hash and user.attributes (name, username, email) to the client, expanding the public API surface of the create endpoint beyond the stated validation intent. Any API consumer or older/alternate client now receives a new payload shape; the email value echoed back is the server-normalized attribute, which the client-side rejectedEmails comparison keys off — the client and server must stay in sync on email normalization or the feature silently fails, an unenforced invariant this diff creates but nothing guarantees.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a persistent write (record.save) from inside model validation, so validating a User mutates the blocked_emails table. Every User#valid?/save with a changed email that matches a row in blocked_emails issues an UPDATE (match_count increment) even when the surrounding transaction rolls back or the record is never persisted; a failed create still counts a 'match', and any code path that calls valid? for inspection (e.g. the new users_controller error branch, specs, background checks) silently corrupts statistics. If the save fails (e.g. lock contention), the exception is unhandled and turns a validation into a 500.

[BUG] The rejectedEmails client-side block is case-sensitive against a server-normalized value: the server pushes user.attributes['email'], which User#email= has downcased, while the client compares it to the raw typed accountEmail. A user typing 'Bad@SpamClub.com' gets result.values.email 'bad@spamclub.com' pushed into rejectedEmails; `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` never matches, so the client-side validation never fires and the user can resubmit the same address indefinitely, getting the generic 'login.errors' flash each time instead of the inline email error the diff was written to provide.

[BUG] The refactor folds email presence/uniqueness and the new EmailValidator into one attribute but the blocked-email check now runs on every save where email_changed?, including updates by existing users, not just account creation. An admin later removes an email from blocked_emails (or sets action_type to do_nothing), but any already-rejected client still has the address in rejectedEmails with no invalidation path — the form blocks the email until a full page reload, so unblocking an email does not take effect for users mid-signup and support cannot clear it without telling them to reload.

[ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload added to the create-failure response has no test coverage anywhere in the diff (no users_controller spec touches the errors/values keys or the client pushObject path). A regression in the response shape (e.g. values.email missing because user.attributes slice changes) would silently degrade the client to the generic flash message — exactly the behavior this PR exists to fix — and no spec would fail; anyone refactoring the controller response later gets bitten.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regexp from the raw setting by only escaping dots, without anchoring or escaping other regex metacharacters that operators can put in email_domains_blacklist/whitelist (e.g. '+', '('), and the BlockedEmail lookup is a plain case-sensitive equality. An operator entering a domain fragment with regex metacharacters gets a RegexpError raised inside validation (500 on signup instead of a 4xx), and a blocked_emails row stored with uppercase (e.g. loaded from an external list) never matches the downcased address User stores — the block silently no-ops for exactly the operators who load the table manually, which the blocked_email_spec comment says is an intended workflow.

[BUG] The entire validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist restriction branches that make up two-thirds of EmailValidator's logic, so the spec verifies the mock, not the validator. The whole email_in_restriction_setting? path (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:15-23), including the regexp escaping and the whitelist/blacklist precedence, is untested: a regression in domain matching or the gsub('.', '\.') escaping ships green, and sites relying on email_domains_blacklist silently stop blocking signups. The two tests that do exist only assert that a stubbed return value of true adds an error and false doesn't — a tautology on the single if-line, true regardless of how should_block? or the restriction settings actually behave.

[ADVISORY] The 'doesn't add an error' test depends on SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist both being blank in the test environment without asserting or setting them, so its pass/fail is coupled to global test-state rather than the behavior under test. If any other spec leaks a whitelist/blacklist SiteSetting (a common cross-spec contamination mode), this test flips to failing or, worse, silently exercises the restriction branch instead of the blocked-email branch, making the suite's green signal untrustworthy for this validator.

[ADVISORY] No test covers the short-circuit 'record.errors[attribute].blank?' guard in EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:16-18), i.e. the interaction between restriction errors and the blocked-email side-effecting call. The untested behavior is that when a whitelist/blacklist error is already present, BlockedEmail.should_block? must NOT be called — but should_block? mutates the DB (increments match_count, stamps last_match_at). A regression that reorders the checks double-counts matches and mangles the operator-facing statistics the blocked_email_spec documents as meaningful (its last_match_at comment), and no spec in this diff would catch it.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff, making the migration inert. The table is created and User validation queries it, but no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or seed_data path ever inserts a BlockedEmail row — operators cannot populate the blocklist, so the entire feature is dead code in production until a later PR adds a writer. The migration itself is reversible (create_table/drop_table), so no data-loss risk; the defect is the inert feature.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (match_count += 1, last_match_at, save) inside model validation, so statistics are written every time any validation runs rather than once per signup attempt. Every call to user.valid? — including client-side re-validation, multiple controller checks within one request, and retries after unrelated validation failures (e.g., short password) — increments match_count and resets last_match_at, corrupting the blocking statistics the model was designed to track. Concurrent requests also race on match_count (lost increments via stale record), and a save failure inside the validator is silently swallowed, returning a stale/false blocking decision.

[ADVISORY] The `email: true` validator (including the BlockedEmail check) is gated on `if: :email_changed?`, so a persisted user whose email was set before this deploy is never checked against the blocklist on save. Any save of an existing user (e.g., profile update, admin edit) that does not alter email skips both the domain-restriction and blocked-email checks entirely; an admin cannot block an address already attached to an account by this mechanism. This matches the previous email_validator gate, so it is not a regression, but the new blocklist feature inherits the gap: rows existing before the blocklist was populated are silently exempt.

[ADVISORY] should_block? increments match_count/last_match_at via record.save with the return value never checked, so a failed save silently drops the statistics update while the signup attempt proceeds and the API reports its normal outcome. Operators relying on match_count/last_match_at to audit blocked-email activity get silently stale/incomplete stats — e.g. under a concurrent uniqueness race (two simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked email both load the row and both save) or any save failure, the count is lost with no log and no error; the operator sees a match that never registered.

[ADVISORY] should_block? (and thus the match_count write) runs on every validation of any record with a changed email, including repeated failed signup attempts and admin edits, so match_count/last_match_at measure validation attempts, not distinct blocked actors. Anyone scripting repeated signup attempts against a blocked address inflates match_count without bound (one DB write per request on the user-validation path — also an unthrottled per-request write amplifier for a request that will be rejected anyway); last_match_at semantics drift from 'when this email was last blocked' to 'when it was last retried', misdirecting abuse investigation.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejection always shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') message for an email the server rejected as blocked, even though the server defines the distinct and more accurate user.email.blocked ('is not allowed'). A user whose email is on the blocklist retries on subsequent attempts and sees only a generic 'invalid email' message that misdescribes the problem, since result.errors.email is available at push time but its message text is discarded; debugging and user self-correction are misdirected toward a syntax error that doesn't exist.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

That validator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) explicitly mutates and persists the matching row (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`). Therefore merely validating a user email causes a persistent write to `blocked_emails`, even if the `User` is never persisted or the surrounding operation fails. This side effect is directly verifiable from the diff and matches the finding’s core concern about silently changing statistics during validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rejectedEmails client-side block is case-sensitive against a server-normalized value: the server pushes user.attributes['email'], which User#email= has downcased, while the client compares it to the raw typed accountEmail. A user typing 'Bad@SpamClub.com' gets result.values.email 'bad@spamclub.com' pushed into rejectedEmails; `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` never matches, so the client-side validation never fires and the user can resubmit the same address indefinitely, getting the generic 'login.errors' flash each time instead of the inline email error the diff was written to provide.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the inline re-validation short-circuits only when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` matches exactly (`contains` is case-sensitive). The array is populated from the server response via `result.values.email` (from `users_controller.rb` returning `user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")`). Because the client compares the raw typed `accountEmail` to a previously returned/stored email string, any case difference between what’s stored/returned and what the user types will prevent a match, allowing repeated submissions without triggering the intended inline email error. The diff shows the strict string comparison and the server-provided value flow; it does not show email normalization, but the case-sensitive mismatch/bypass is still present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The refactor folds email presence/uniqueness and the new EmailValidator into one attribute but the blocked-email check now runs on every save where email_changed?, including updates by existing users, not just account creation. An admin later removes an email from blocked_emails (or sets action_type to do_nothing), but any already-rejected client still has the address in rejectedEmails with no invalidation path — the form blocks the email until a full page reload, so unblocking an email does not take effect for users mid-signup and support cannot clear it without telling them to reload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds client-side caching of server-rejected emails in `create_account_controller.js` (`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])`), and `emailValidation` now hard-fails any email in that list (`if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)) ... failed: true`). The list is only ever appended to on a failed create (`pushObject(result.values.email)`) and is never cleared/invalidated, so if the server-side block is later removed, a user mid-signup will still be prevented from using that email until a full reload/controller reset. The claim about the validator running on any `email_changed?` save is true, but that condition already existed before the refactor; the verifiable regression here is the sticky `rejectedEmails` behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload added to the create-failure response has no test coverage anywhere in the diff (no users_controller spec touches the errors/values keys or the client pushObject path). A regression in the response shape (e.g. values.email missing because user.attributes slice changes) would silently degrade the client to the generic flash message — exactly the behavior this PR exists to fix — and no spec would fail; anyone refactoring the controller response later gets bitten.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new response keys in UsersController#create failure JSON (`errors: user.errors.to_hash`, `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`) and new client behavior that depends on them (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`). The only added specs cover `BlockedEmail` and `EmailValidator`; there is no controller/request spec asserting the presence/shape of `errors`/`values`, nor any JS test covering the `rejectedEmails`/`pushObject` path. A future change to the response shape (e.g., `values.email` missing) would not be caught by tests and would silently disable the new client-side rejection behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regexp from the raw setting by only escaping dots, without anchoring or escaping other regex metacharacters that operators can put in email_domains_blacklist/whitelist (e.g. '+', '('), and the BlockedEmail lookup is a plain case-sensitive equality. An operator entering a domain fragment with regex metacharacters gets a RegexpError raised inside validation (500 on signup instead of a 4xx), and a blocked_emails row stored with uppercase (e.g. loaded from an external list) never matches the downcased address User stores — the block silently no-ops for exactly the operators who load the table manually, which the blocked_email_spec comment says is an intended workflow.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? constructs Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) from a SiteSetting value after only gsub('.', '\\.'). This leaves other regex metacharacters unescaped and unvalidated, so an operator-provided setting containing invalid regex (e.g., unmatched '(') would raise RegexpError during validation with no rescue in validate_each, breaking signup. Separately, BlockedEmail.should_block? does a direct where(email: email).first lookup with no normalization; in a case-sensitive DB this will not match manually-loaded blocked_emails entries with different casing than the provided email, making blocking silently ineffective in that scenario.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The entire validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist restriction branches that make up two-thirds of EmailValidator's logic, so the spec verifies the mock, not the validator. The whole email_in_restriction_setting? path (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:15-23), including the regexp escaping and the whitelist/blacklist precedence, is untested: a regression in domain matching or the gsub('.', '\.') escaping ships green, and sites relying on email_domains_blacklist silently stop blocking signups. The two tests that do exist only assert that a stubbed return value of true adds an error and false doesn't — a tautology on the single if-line, true regardless of how should_block? or the restriction settings actually behave.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new EmailValidator with three major behaviors: (1) whitelist domain restriction, (2) blacklist domain restriction, and (3) BlockedEmail.should_block? (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The new spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only covers the blocked-email behavior and does so by stubbing BlockedEmail.should_block? to return true/false, which means it never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branches or the regex-based email_in_restriction_setting? matching/escaping logic. This is a concrete, diff-grounded testing gap (untested branches and precedence), but it is not itself a runtime defect proven by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 'doesn't add an error' test depends on SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist and email_domains_blacklist both being blank in the test environment without asserting or setting them, so its pass/fail is coupled to global test-state rather than the behavior under test. If any other spec leaks a whitelist/blacklist SiteSetting (a common cross-spec contamination mode), this test flips to failing or, worse, silently exercises the restriction branch instead of the blocked-email branch, making the suite's green signal untrustworthy for this validator.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the "doesn't add an error" example only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and then asserts record.errors[:email] is blank. But EmailValidator#validate_each first consults SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist and can add a :user.email.not_allowed error before it ever reaches the blocked-email logic. The spec does not set or assert those SiteSettings are blank, so its outcome is coupled to global SiteSetting state that could be altered by other specs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test covers the short-circuit 'record.errors[attribute].blank?' guard in EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:16-18), i.e. the interaction between restriction errors and the blocked-email side-effecting call. The untested behavior is that when a whitelist/blacklist error is already present, BlockedEmail.should_block? must NOT be called — but should_block? mutates the DB (increments match_count, stamps last_match_at). A regression that reorders the checks double-counts matches and mangles the operator-facing statistics the blocked_email_spec documents as meaningful (its last_match_at comment), and no spec in this diff would catch it.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is guarded by `record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lines ~16-18 in the new file), which is meant to avoid calling `should_block?` when whitelist/blacklist validation has already added an error. The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests the blocked-email branch by stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, and does not cover the interaction where a restriction error is present and `should_block?` must *not* be invoked (important because `BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates DB stats as tested in `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`). This is a concrete, diff-grounded missing-test concern rather than a current functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in this diff, making the migration inert. The table is created and User validation queries it, but no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or seed_data path ever inserts a BlockedEmail row — operators cannot populate the blocklist, so the entire feature is dead code in production until a later PR adds a writer. The migration itself is reversible (create_table/drop_table), so no data-loss risk; the defect is the inert feature.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `blocked_emails` table + `BlockedEmail` model and wires it into `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within this diff there is no code path to create/manage `BlockedEmail` rows (no controller/admin UI/rake task/seed shown). That makes the new blocking behavior effectively unusable unless populated manually outside the app, which is an incompleteness/operational gap rather than a direct correctness bug in the added code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (match_count += 1, last_match_at, save) inside model validation, so statistics are written every time any validation runs rather than once per signup attempt. Every call to user.valid? — including client-side re-validation, multiple controller checks within one request, and retries after unrelated validation failures (e.g., short password) — increments match_count and resets last_match_at, corrupting the blocking statistics the model was designed to track. Concurrent requests also race on match_count (lost increments via stale record), and a save failure inside the validator is silently swallowed, returning a stale/false blocking decision.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a side-effecting validation: `User` now uses `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does a read-modify-write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `save`) every time the validator runs. For a new/unsaved user, `email_changed?` remains true across repeated `valid?` calls, so multiple validations within a single signup flow can increment `match_count` and update `last_match_at` multiple times, corrupting the intended “attempt” statistics. The increment is also non-atomic (`match_count += 1` then `save`), so concurrent validations can lose updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `email: true` validator (including the BlockedEmail check) is gated on `if: :email_changed?`, so a persisted user whose email was set before this deploy is never checked against the blocklist on save. Any save of an existing user (e.g., profile update, admin edit) that does not alter email skips both the domain-restriction and blocked-email checks entirely; an admin cannot block an address already attached to an account by this mechanism. This matches the previous email_validator gate, so it is not a regression, but the new blocklist feature inherits the gap: rows existing before the blocklist was populated are silently exempt.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb`, the new validator `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` gates *all* logic in `EmailValidator`, including the `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` check. Therefore, on saves where a persisted user's email is unchanged, neither domain restriction checks nor the new blocklist check will run. This matches the previous behavior (`validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`), so it’s not a regression, but it is a real scope gap for the new blocklist feature (it won’t affect already-attached emails unless the email field changes).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? increments match_count/last_match_at via record.save with the return value never checked, so a failed save silently drops the statistics update while the signup attempt proceeds and the API reports its normal outcome. Operators relying on match_count/last_match_at to audit blocked-email activity get silently stale/incomplete stats — e.g. under a concurrent uniqueness race (two simultaneous signup attempts for the same blocked email both load the row and both save) or any save failure, the count is lost with no log and no error; the operator sees a match that never registered.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `should_block?` does `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` and ignores the boolean result of `save`. From the diff, blocking behavior depends only on `record.action_type`, so a failed save would not change the API outcome (still blocks/does_nothing), but it would silently fail to persist the statistics update (`match_count`/`last_match_at`). Also, the increment is non-atomic (read/modify/write), so concurrent calls can lose increments. This is a concrete, diff-grounded robustness/auditability issue rather than a directly user-visible correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? (and thus the match_count write) runs on every validation of any record with a changed email, including repeated failed signup attempts and admin edits, so match_count/last_match_at measure validation attempts, not distinct blocked actors. Anyone scripting repeated signup attempts against a blocked address inflates match_count without bound (one DB write per request on the user-validation path — also an unthrottled per-request write amplifier for a request that will be rejected anyway); last_match_at semantics drift from 'when this email was last blocked' to 'when it was last retried', misdirecting abuse investigation.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` whenever there are no prior email errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new model) performs a DB write (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) on every call if a matching record exists. Because `User` now runs this validator on `email_changed?` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), repeated failed signups or edits using a blocked email will repeatedly trigger these writes, inflating `match_count`/`last_match_at` and creating an unthrottled per-request write amplifier on a path that will be rejected anyway.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejection always shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') message for an email the server rejected as blocked, even though the server defines the distinct and more accurate user.email.blocked ('is not allowed'). A user whose email is on the blocklist retries on subsequent attempts and sees only a generic 'invalid email' message that misdescribes the problem, since result.errors.email is available at push time but its message text is discarded; debugging and user self-correction are misdirected toward a syntax error that doesn't exist.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, when an email is in `rejectedEmails`, the validation always returns `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (generic) regardless of why the server rejected it. Yet the server now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` (users_controller.rb) and the new EmailValidator can add the specific `'user.email.blocked'` message (server.en.yml + lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The client pushes only `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` and discards `result.errors.email`, so a blocklisted email will be labeled “invalid” on subsequent attempts, misdescribing the server-side blocked condition.
